items.title: Bridging Alloy and OpenTelemetry: the OTel engine is now in Public Preview
items.summary: Many Grafana Cloud customers love what Alloy offers them, but we're also seeing a growing base of users who feel the same way about the OpenTelemetry Collector. We want to make it easy for customers to make the decision that makes the most sense, regardless of their preference.When we introduced the OpenTelemetry engine for Grafana Alloy, we set out to give teams a way to run native OTLP pipelines without giving up the power and flexibility Alloy is known for. Since then we've kept building: ironing out service installation support, enabling Fleet Management, and folding in feedback from early users. Today, as of Alloy v1.21.0, we're happy to share that the OTel engine has moved into Public Preview, running right alongside the default engine you already know. In this post, we'll dig into when you'd reach for each engine, walk through some of the most interesting use cases we've seen so far, and give a preview of where both engines are headed next.The motivation behind each engineBefore diving into specific new features, let’s recap why we have two engines in Alloy.Default engineThe default engine is a cross-ecosystem engine at its core; it's not tied to any single wire format or vendor. It can just as easily run a Prometheus pipeline, an OTLP pipeline, or a Loki pipeline, all defined using Alloy's own configuration syntax. That flexibility is what makes it a Swiss army knife: the same engine that scrapes Prometheus metrics can pull in logs over syslog for logs, ingest OTLP, scrape Prometheus metrics from embedded exporters, and route all of it to wherever it needs to go.OpenTelemetry engine There's a lot to like about being able to speak every ecosystem's language. But the telemetry landscape itself is moving in the opposite direction. Rather than translating between formats, the industry is increasingly converging on a single, shared model defined by the OpenTelemetry specification. That's what an OpenTelemetry Collector actually is: a pipeline that treats OTLP as the native format end-to-end, prioritizing portability and open standards over ecosystem-bridging translation. At its core, Alloy's OTel engine is Grafana Labs' own distribution of the OpenTelemetry Collector.Running the OTel engineIt's just a collector The OTel engine is an OpenTelemetry Collector distribution that ships inside Alloy. It runs standard collector YAML with no translation and no Alloy syntax. If you already have a collector config, you already have an OTel engine config.- otelcol --config=config.yaml+ alloy otel --config=config.yamlThe rest of the CLI matches, too. validate, components, print-config, and --set all work the way they do upstream, so scripts and CI that call otelcol validate keep working.The same goes for the tools you deploy collectors with. On the upstream Helm chart, it's two values:image:  repository: grafana/alloycommand:  name: "bin/otelcol"The OpenTelemetry Operator used to fail on the Alloy image because it had no way to set the container command. We added spec.command upstream (Operator v0.153.0 and later), so now it's one line:spec:  image: grafana/alloy:  command: ["/bin/alloy", "otel"]For a non-containerized installation, the Alloy packages can run either engine as a service. Set ALLOY_OTEL_MODE=1 and the service runs the OTel engine against config.yaml. Read our docs for more information on how to set it up by platform.Fleet management Managing collector configuration by hand doesn't scale past a handful of hosts, so remote configuration was one of the first gaps we closed after the initial release. As of Alloy v1.19.0, you can manage OTel engine configuration centrally with Fleet Management. The OpAMP supervisor is embedded in the Alloy binary and runs through the new experimental otel-supervisor subcommand: point it at your Fleet Management endpoint and credentials with a supervisor configuration file, and Alloy handles the connection, pulls down your pipeline configuration, and applies changes as you publish them. See the Alloy otel-supervisor reference to get started.An escape hatch: the alloyengine extensionSometimes the component you need only exists in the default engine today. The alloyengine extension runs Alloy configuration inside the same collector process, so you can pick up that one piece without running a second agent.It's Experimental, and we expect it to stay that way. The two engines run side by side but can't pass data to each other directly, so anything that crosses over goes out over the network, usually OTLP.If you reach for it, tell us why. Open an issue on the Alloy repo with the component you needed. That list is how we decide which default engine pieces become native OpenTelemetry collector components next.Experiments with Grafana Cloud productsHeads up first: nothing in this section is supported, and you shouldn't run it in production.
